Time and Effort Defined

From the ORA eTraining module "Show Your Work: Understanding Time and Effort Reporting" (lesson 1 of 8).
What is Effort Reporting?
What is Time and Effort Reporting?
Time and Effort Reporting is the formal process by which an institution verifies that the salary and wages charged to sponsored projects reasonably reflects the proportion of an individual's total institutional work devoted to those projects. It is not a record of hours worked, but a certification of effort as a percentage of total activities including research, teaching, and administrative duties.
Auditor Assurance
Effort reporting provides sufficient assurance to state and federal auditors that appropriate internal control measures actively track allocability for each sponsored project. Auditors are looking for: (1) documentation support (2) reasonableness (3) timeliness and (4) internal controls.
Federally Mandated
Effort reporting is a federally mandated requirement outlined in Code of Federal Regulations (CFR). Under which, we in the research administration reference Uniform Guidance (2CFR200) as our playbook for research compliance. 2CFR200.430 specifically details personnel compensation and effort on sponsored projects.

Common Compliance Risks
https://cdn.articulate.com/assets/rise/assets/block-defaults/mountains_thumb.jpg
Salary charged to federal awards should not exceed stated effort commitments outlined in the project proposal submission packet.
Salary Charged > Effort Performed
Effort commitments for project personnel outlined in the approved Notice of Award must be met. Significant deviation from stated effort (typically more than 25%) will required sponsor/agency review and approval.
Effort Committed but Not Met
Effort certification is federally required to be completed on at least an annual basis. Increased frequency is allowed at the institution's discretion. All effort certification requests should be verified and completed within a timely manner.
Late Certifications
Those who certify effort records need to have first-hand knowledge of the employee's effort.
